Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

derivations.claim: Normalize $\widehat v:=v/\|v\|_2$. Then $\|J\widehat v-\theta\widehat v\|_2=\|Jv-\theta v\|_2/\|v\|_2\le\rho/s$. Expand $\widehat v=\sum_{k=1}^m c_ku_k$ in the orthonormal basis [F1]. Then $\|J\widehat v-\theta\widehat v\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_k^2(\lambda_k-\theta)^2 \ge g^2\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2.$ Thus $\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2\le\rho^2/(s^2g^2)$.

Put $\varepsilon=1$ if $c_i\ge0$ and $\varepsilon=-1$ otherwise. Since $\widehat v$ and $u_i$ are unit vectors, $\|\widehat v-\varepsilon u_i\|_2^2=2(1-|c_i|)\le2(1-c_i^2)=2\sum_{k\ne i}c_k^2\le2\rho^2/(s^2g^2)$.

By [F4], $\widehat v_1^2\le\sum_{k=1}^m\widehat v_k^2=1$ and $(u_i)_1^2\le\sum_{k=1}^m(u_i)_k^2=1$, since all coordinate squares are nonnegative. Hence $|\widehat v_1|,|(u_i)_1|\le1$. Therefore $|\widehat v_1^2-(u_i)_1^2| =|\widehat v_1-\varepsilon(u_i)_1|\,|\widehat v_1+\varepsilon(u_i)_1| \le2\|\widehat v-\varepsilon u_i\|_2 \le2\sqrt2\,\rho/(sg).$
Since $\widehat v_1^2=v_1^2/\|v\|_2^2$, multiply step 3.1 by $\mu_0>0$ from [F2] and use [F3]. The result is the claimed Gaussian weight bound.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$
\ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j}
$$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$
w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad
Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i)
$$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in

\int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i).
$$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$
S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\}
$$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

$Q_j(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}w_i^{(j)}f(x_i^{(j)})$ be a well-defined Gaussian rule

[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]]. Its **tensor-product
quadrature rule** is
$$
Q_{\otimes}(f):=
\sum_{i_1=1}^{m_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{m_d}
\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}w_{i_j}^{(j)}\right)
f\left(x_{i_1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{i_d}^{(d)}\right).
$$
Its node set is the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional node sets; the
displayed finite sum is its value on any function defined on that node set.

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite coefficient family $(c_\alpha)$ indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$
P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}.
$$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$
I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}.
$$
The coefficient family is part of the formal polynomial data, so this finite
sum is unambiguous. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$
Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P).
$$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.
